## Text Functions and Operators

This section describes functions and operators for examining and manipulating [`STRING` values](../../sql/data_types/text.md).

<!-- Start of section generated by scripts/generate_sql_function_docs.py; categories: [string, regex] -->
<!-- markdownlint-disable MD056 -->

| Function                                                                                                                | Description                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
| :---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | :---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| [`string[index]`](#stringindex)                                                                                         | Extracts a single character using a (1-based) `index`.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              |
| [`string[begin:end]`](#stringbeginend)                                                                                  | Extracts a string using [slice conventions](../../sql/functions/list.md#slicing) similar to Python. Missing `begin` or `end` arguments are interpreted as the beginning or end of the list respectively. Negative values are accepted.                                                                                                                                              |
| [`string LIKE target`](#string-like-target)                                                                             | Returns `true` if the `string` matches the like specifier (see [Pattern Matching](../../sql/functions/pattern_matching/index.md)).                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| [`string SIMILAR TO regex`](#string-similar-to-regex)                                                                   | Returns `true` if the `string` matches the `regex` (see [Pattern Matching](../../sql/functions/pattern_matching/index.md)).                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |

| <a href="#arg1--arg2"><code>arg1 &#124;&#124; arg2</code></a>                                                           | Concatenates two strings, lists, or blobs. Any `NULL` input results in `NULL`. See also [`concat(arg1, arg2, ...)`](../../sql/functions/text.md#concatvalue-) and [`list_concat(list1, list2, ...)`](../../sql/functions/list.md#list_concatlist_1--list_n).                                                                                                                        |
| [`array_extract(string, index)`](#array_extractstring-index)                                                            | Extracts a single character from a `string` using a (1-based) `index`.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              |

Negative values are accepted.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |

<!-- markdownlint-enable MD056 -->

#### `string[index]`

Extracts a single character using a (1-based) `index`. Alias: `array_extract`.

<SqlLogicTest id="sql/functions/text/string_index" />

#### `string[begin:end]`

Extracts a string using [slice conventions](../../sql/functions/list.md#slicing) similar to Python. Missing `begin` or `end` arguments are interpreted as the beginning or end of the list respectively. Negative values are accepted. Alias: `array_slice`.

<SqlLogicTest id="sql/functions/text/string_begin_end" />

#### `string LIKE target`

Returns `true` if the `string` matches the like specifier (see [Pattern Matching](../../sql/functions/pattern_matching/index.md)).

<SqlLogicTest id="sql/functions/text/string_like_target" />

#### `string SIMILAR TO regex`

Returns `true` if the `string` matches the `regex` (see [Pattern Matching](../../sql/functions/pattern_matching/index.md)). Alias: `regexp_full_match`.

<SqlLogicTest id="sql/functions/text/string_similar_to_regex" />

#### `arg1 || arg2`

Concatenates two strings, lists, or blobs. Any `NULL` input results in `NULL`. See also [`concat(arg1, arg2, ...)`](../../sql/functions/text.md#concatvalue-) and [`list_concat(list1, list2, ...)`](../../sql/functions/list.md#list_concatlist_1--list_n).

<SqlLogicTest id="sql/functions/text/string_concat_op" />

#### `array_extract(string, index)`

Extracts a single character from a `string` using a (1-based) `index`.

<SqlLogicTest id="sql/functions/text/array_extract" />

#### `array_slice(list, begin, end)`

Extracts a sublist or substring using [slice conventions](../../sql/functions/list.md#slicing). Negative values are accepted. Alias: `list_slice`.

<SqlLogicTest id="sql/functions/text/array_slice" />

#### `ascii(string)`

Returns an integer that represents the Unicode code point of the first character of the `string`.

<SqlLogicTest id="sql/functions/text/ascii" />

#### `bar(x, min, max[, width])`

Draws a band whose width is proportional to (`x - min`) and equal to `width` characters when `x` = `max`. `width` defaults to 80.

<SqlLogicTest id="sql/functions/text/bar" />

#### `bin(string)`

Converts the `string` to binary representation. Alias: `to_binary`.

<SqlLogicTest id="sql/functions/text/bin" />

#### `bit_length(string)`

Number of bits in a `string`.

<SqlLogicTest id="sql/functions/text/bit_length" />

#### `chr(code_point)`

Returns a character which is corresponding the ASCII code value or Unicode code point.

<SqlLogicTest id="sql/functions/text/chr" />

#### `concat(value, ...)`

Concatenates multiple strings or lists. `NULL` inputs are skipped. See also <a href="#arg1--arg2">operator <code>&#124;&#124;</code></a>.

If `trim_extension` is `true`, the file extension will be removed (defaults to `false`). `separator` options: `system`, `both_slash` (default), `forward_slash`, `backslash`.

A table function that returns the content from `source` (a filename, a list of filenames, or a glob pattern); query it with `FROM`. It yields `filename`, `content`, `size` and `last_modified` columns, with `content` as a `VARCHAR`. The file content is first validated to be valid UTF-8. If `read_text` attempts to read a file with invalid UTF-8 an error is thrown suggesting to use `read_blob` instead. See the [`read_text` guide](../../cookbook/file_formats/read_file.md#read_text) for more details.

#### `regexp_extract(string, regex[, group][, options])`

If `string` contains the `regex` pattern, returns the capturing group specified by optional parameter `group`; otherwise, returns the empty string. The `group` must be a constant value. If no `group` is given, it defaults to 0. A set of optional [regex `options`](../../sql/functions/regular_expressions.md#options-for-regular-expression-functions) can be set.

If `string` contains the `regex` pattern, returns the capturing groups as a struct with corresponding names from `name_list`; otherwise, returns a struct with the same keys and empty strings as values. A set of optional [regex `options`](../../sql/functions/regular_expressions.md#options-for-regular-expression-functions) can be set.

Finds non-overlapping occurrences of the `regex` in the `string` and returns the corresponding values of the capturing `group`. A set of optional [regex `options`](../../sql/functions/regular_expressions.md#options-for-regular-expression-functions) can be set.

## Text Similarity Functions

These functions are used to measure the similarity of two strings using various [similarity measures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Similarity_measure).

<!-- Start of section generated by scripts/generate_sql_function_docs.py; categories: [text_similarity] -->
<!-- markdownlint-disable MD056 -->

| :---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | :-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| [`damerau_levenshtein(s1, s2)`](#damerau_levenshteins1-s2)                                      | Extension of Levenshtein distance to also include transposition of adjacent characters as an allowed edit operation. In other words, the minimum number of edit operations (insertions, deletions, substitutions or transpositions) required to change one string to another. Characters of different cases (e.g., `a` and `A`) are considered different. |
| [`editdist3(s1, s2)`](#levenshteins1-s2)                                                        | Alias for `levenshtein`.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| [`hamming(s1, s2)`](#hammings1-s2)                                                              | The Hamming distance between two strings, i.e., the number of positions with different characters for two strings of equal length. Strings must be of equal length. Characters of different cases (e.g., `a` and `A`) are considered different.                                                                                                           |
| [`jaccard(s1, s2)`](#jaccards1-s2)                                                              | The Jaccard similarity between two strings. Characters of different cases (e.g., `a` and `A`) are considered different. Returns a number between 0 and 1.                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
| [`jaro_similarity(s1, s2[, score_cutoff])`](#jaro_similaritys1-s2-score_cutoff)                 | The Jaro similarity between two strings. Characters of different cases (e.g., `a` and `A`) are considered different. Returns a number between 0 and 1. Characters of different cases (e.g., `a` and `A`) are considered different. Returns a number between 0 and 1. For similarity < `score_cutoff`, 0 is returned instead. `score_cutoff` defaults to 0.                                                                                                      |
| [`levenshtein(s1, s2)`](#levenshteins1-s2)                                                      | The minimum number of single-character edits (insertions, deletions or substitutions) required to change one string to the other. Characters of different cases (e.g., `a` and `A`) are considered different.                                                                                                                                             |

<!-- markdownlint-enable MD056 -->

#### `damerau_levenshtein(s1, s2)`

Extension of Levenshtein distance to also include transposition of adjacent characters as an allowed edit operation. In other words, the minimum number of edit operations (insertions, deletions, substitutions or transpositions) required to change one string to another. Characters of different cases (e.g., `a` and `A`) are considered different.

<SqlLogicTest id="sql/functions/text/damerau_levenshtein" />

#### `hamming(s1, s2)`

The Hamming distance between two strings, i.e., the number of positions with different characters for two strings of equal length. Strings must be of equal length. Characters of different cases (e.g., `a` and `A`) are considered different. Alias: `mismatches`.

<SqlLogicTest id="sql/functions/text/hamming" />

#### `jaccard(s1, s2)`

The Jaccard similarity between two strings. Characters of different cases (e.g., `a` and `A`) are considered different. Returns a number between 0 and 1.

<SqlLogicTest id="sql/functions/text/jaccard" />

#### `jaro_similarity(s1, s2[, score_cutoff])`

The Jaro similarity between two strings. Characters of different cases (e.g., `a` and `A`) are considered different. Returns a number between 0 and 1. For similarity < `score_cutoff`, 0 is returned instead. `score_cutoff` defaults to 0.

<SqlLogicTest id="sql/functions/text/jaro_similarity" />

#### `jaro_winkler_similarity(s1, s2[, score_cutoff])`

The Jaro-Winkler similarity between two strings. Characters of different cases (e.g., `a` and `A`) are considered different. Returns a number between 0 and 1. For similarity < `score_cutoff`, 0 is returned instead. `score_cutoff` defaults to 0.

<SqlLogicTest id="sql/functions/text/jaro_winkler_similarity" />

#### `levenshtein(s1, s2)`

The minimum number of single-character edits (insertions, deletions or substitutions) required to change one string to the other. Characters of different cases (e.g., `a` and `A`) are considered different. Alias: `editdist3`.

<SqlLogicTest id="sql/functions/text/levenshtein" />

## Formatters

### `format` Syntax

The `format(format, ...)` function formats a string using PostgreSQL-style [`format`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/functions-string.html#FUNCTIONS-STRING-FORMAT) specifiers — each specifier in `format` is replaced by the corresponding argument. (This is PostgreSQL's `format`, not the `{}`-placeholder syntax of the `{fmt}` library.)

A specifier has the form `%[position$][-][width]type`, where `type` is one of:

| Type | Description |
| :--- | :--- |
| `%s` | The argument as a string. |
| `%I` | The argument as a quoted SQL identifier (double-quoted when needed). |
| `%L` | The argument as a quoted SQL literal (single-quoted, embedded quotes escaped; `NULL` becomes `NULL`). |
| `%%` | A literal `%` (consumes no argument). |

Only `s`, `I` and `L` are valid types — any other (e.g. `%d`) raises `unrecognized format() type specifier`.

Basic substitution with `%s`:

<SqlLogicTest id="sql/functions/text/format" />

`%I` and `%L` safely quote identifiers and literals — useful for building SQL dynamically:

<SqlLogicTest id="sql/functions/text/format_identifier_literal" />

Arguments are consumed in order; an explicit position can be given as `%n$` (e.g. `%1$s`), which also lets you reuse and reorder them:

<SqlLogicTest id="sql/functions/text/format_positional" />

An optional minimum field `width` right-justifies the value (left-justifies with a leading `-`), padding with spaces:

<SqlLogicTest id="sql/functions/text/format_width" />

### `printf` Syntax

The `printf(format, parameters...)` function formats strings using the [`printf` syntax](https://cplusplus.com/reference/cstdio/printf/).

Format a string using positional arguments `%position$formatter`, e.g., the second parameter as a string is encoded as `%2$s`:

#### Format Specifiers

| Specifier | Description                                                  | Example        |
| :-------- | :----------------------------------------------------------- | :------------- |
| `%c`      | character code to character                                  | `a`            |
| `%d`      | integer                                                      | `654321`       |
| `%E`      | scientific notation                                          | `3.141593E+00` |
| `%f`      | float                                                        | `4.560000`     |
| `%hd`     | integer truncated to a C `short`                             | `-1039`        |
| `%hhd`    | integer truncated to a C `signed char`                       | `-15`          |
| `%lld`    | integer                                                      | `654321`       |
| `%o`      | octal                                                        | `2375761`      |
| `%s`      | string                                                       | `asd`          |
| `%x`      | hexadecimal                                                  | `9fbf1`        |

`printf` does not support thousand-separator specifiers (such as `%,d`, `%_d` or `%''d`); they raise `invalid format specifier`:
